plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.

elements: 3×3×3 array of small red spheres representing atoms (27 total)
thin black lines along all cube edges and nearest-neighbor rows forming the open cubic lattice
translucent teal plane cutting through the lattice, parallel to a cube face in the (100) orientation
same teal plane tilted diagonally in the (110) orientation, slicing from lower-left to upper-right
highlighted atoms lying on the active plane (spheres brighten slightly)
plane spacing label d showing the perpendicular gap between adjacent planes of the family

interactions.teaches: Rotating the lattice reveals that the shaded sheet is a genuine 2D plane slicing through a 3D array of atoms, not just a painted square

interactions.label: Plane family
interactions.teaches: One crystal contains many families of atomic planes at different orientations — switching the family rotates the shaded sheet through the same fixed lattice

interactions.label: Adjacent plane
interactions.teaches: Each family is a stack of parallel, equally spaced planes; stepping between them shows which rows of atoms each sheet contains and reveals the spacing d that sets the Bragg diffraction angle

demo_steps.title: Face-parallel planes
demo_steps.narration: The teal sheet lies parallel to a cube face and passes through the middle sheet of atoms. Atoms on the plane highlight.

demo_steps.title: Step to a neighboring plane
demo_steps.narration: Sliding the index shifts the sheet to the adjacent parallel plane — a different row of atoms, same orientation, separated by spacing d.

demo_steps.title: Diagonal family
demo_steps.narration: Switching to (110) tilts the plane diagonally through the same lattice. The intersected atoms and the spacing d both change — each family diffracts at its own angle.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cubic lattice: 27 red spheres (#cc2222, radius ~0.12) at integer coordinates {0,1,2}³, so cube side = 2 world units; camera fits ±2. Black lines (#222, thin cylinders) along every nearest-neighbor row in x, y, z — 9 lines per axis direction, 27 total. Teal plane (#2a9d8f, opacity 0.35, double-sided): for (100), an x = k plane of size 2.2×2.2 (k = planeIndex+1, i.e. x = 0,1,2); for (110), the plane x + y = c with c = planeIndex+2 (c = 1,2,3), clipped to the cube, giving a diagonal sheet from lower-left to upper-right as in the right source panel. Plane spacing: d(100) = a = 1 unit; d(110) = a/√2 ≈ 0.707 — the (110) sheet should visibly cut through atom centers along a diagonal. The source shows two cubes side by side; render ONE cube and use the toggle to reproduce both views, per multi-panel rule.
interactionPlan.notes: Highlight atoms whose coordinates satisfy the current plane equation (within epsilon) by raising emissive intensity. Clip the (110) plane polygon to the cube bounds by intersecting x+y=c with the 0..2 box. Show the d label with a short perpendicular double-arrow between the active plane and the ghost of its neighbor (render neighbor as faint outline, opacity 0.12). Keep lattice static when toggling family so orientation is the only variable.

authoredContext:
Although the figure depicts a crystal as a two-dimensional array of scattering centers for simplicity, real crystals are structures in three dimensions. Scattering can occur simultaneously from different families of planes at different orientations and spacing patterns known as called Bragg planes, as shown in the figure. The resulting interference pattern can be quite complex.

Because of the regularity that makes a crystal structure, one crystal can have many families of planes within its geometry, each one giving rise to X-ray diffraction.

Figure shows two crystal lattices, with atoms shown as small circles, connected to each other by lines. In the first lattice, flat planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In the second, slanted planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In each case, the planes are seen as a combination of different atoms in the same lattice.
